directive: The new Roman-authorized expedition continues beyond the engineered route, with Valerius investigating how such substantial roadwork could have escaped ordinary Roman notice and sending his private suspicion to Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer while established estate administration, correspondence, agricultural management, and documentary inquiry continue independently.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION RETURNS TO THE ENGINEERED ROUTE AND BEGINS A MORE DELIBERATE SURVEY
events.body: The expedition leaves its temporary camp and returns to the exposed engineered route rather than treating yesterday's discovery as a curiosity to be passed over. The companions clear only enough vegetation and loose earth to establish the visible course without claiming that buried sections are known. The scribes begin a separate survey sheet for construction features, recording drainage, stone placement, grades, and interruptions as observations rather than assigning an origin. The party follows the route far enough to establish that the engineered work continues beyond the first inspected corridor. Provisions are consumed by the additional halt-and-survey work, but the expedition's manpower and military organization remain unchanged. By evening Valerius has ordered that the route receive greater investigative attention during the next stage of the expedition.

events.title: COMPARISON OF THE ROADWORK REVEALS A CONSISTENT METHOD ACROSS SEPARATE SECTIONS
events.body: A second comparison of exposed sections shows that the drainage and roadbed treatment is not confined to one convenient patch of ground. The scribes identify recurring construction features while keeping the regional anchors around Narnia, Interamna Nahars, Spoletium, Fulginium, and Iguvium separate from any claim about the road's builder or ultimate destination. The finding strengthens the expedition's reason to investigate the corridor as a coherent engineered work rather than a collection of unrelated repairs. No inscription, milestone, or official Roman marker is recovered that would establish who commissioned it. The absence of such evidence becomes part of the investigation rather than a reason to fill the gap with speculation.

events.title: THE ROAD'S SILENCE FORCES VALERIUS TO CONFRONT AN UNSETTLING QUESTION
events.body:
The next morning you return to the road before the column is fully assembled, carrying the previous day's notes with you rather than waiting for the scribes to finish copying them.
You walk the exposed surface slowly, looking less at where it leads than at what kind of administration would normally have left evidence around a work of this quality.
The drainage is not merely a ditch cut where water happened to run. In the sections you can inspect, the builders repeatedly solved the same problem in ways that suggest planning rather than improvisation.
The roadbed has also survived in places where an ordinary local track should have broken apart under weather, traffic, and neglect. You cannot yet say how old the work is, but you can say that it was made to endure.
You ask the scribes to compare every observed feature with the route register already built during the expedition. The question is no longer simply where the road goes.
The question is why a road capable of supporting organized movement has left so little recognizable trace in the Roman administrative record available to your expedition.
You are careful not to turn absence of evidence into proof. A missing record could have many causes, and the field register is written accordingly.
Yet the thought refuses to leave you. If this country is within Roman territory and a substantial engineered corridor lies here, then either the work predates the administrative arrangements now familiar to Rome, has fallen outside the attention of the authorities, or has been maintained by people who do not appear in the records you expected to find.
You stop beside a section where the road disappears under a bank of earth and examine the ground above it. The concealment is not enough to prove deliberate hiding, but it makes the possibility impossible to ignore.
A companion suggests that the route may simply be an old local work that survived after the authorities ceased using it. You record the suggestion because it is reasonable.
But another possibility weighs more heavily on you: a population capable of maintaining such a corridor could have reasons for avoiding the notice of officials.
You think of deserters, fugitives, displaced groups, and isolated communities that might survive beyond the normal reach of Roman administration. None of those possibilities is yet demonstrated here.
Still, the physical evidence gives the suspicion a different character than it had when it was only a thought. There is now a real engineered corridor requiring an explanation.
You order the party to inspect side tracks, water points, concealed approaches, and places where a traveler could leave the main route without being immediately visible from it.
The investigation finds no massed population and no military force. What it finds instead are traces of repeated passage, old clearings, and interruptions in the road's visible course that deserve to be recorded.
The scribes begin a separate section titled for the question of administrative oversight. You insist that the heading describe the question, not assert an answer.
As the afternoon passes, you consider the Roman consequence if your suspicion were ever confirmed. A hidden community composed of deserters or fugitives would not merely be an obscure local curiosity.
Such a community could know the terrain, possess established supply points, evade ordinary patrol patterns, and potentially attract additional fugitives from elsewhere.
That would make the matter one of Roman security as much as geography, but you refuse to exaggerate the danger in the dispatch you intend to send. A suspicion must remain a suspicion until evidence gives it weight.
Before dusk you order the scribes to preserve both the physical observations and the uncertainty surrounding their interpretation. The road has become more important precisely because it cannot yet explain itself.
You spend the final light looking along the engineered line toward the folds of country beyond the inspected section, aware that the expedition may have found not merely an old road but a clue to something living beyond the administrative map.
The column settles for the night with the route register enlarged and the question sharper than before. You have not discovered deserters, a marooned community, or any hidden polity; you have discovered a circumstance that makes those possibilities worth investigating seriously.

classification_audit.reason: The expedition's sustained investigation of an unexplained engineered corridor and the personally experienced security question surrounding its apparent administrative absence constitute an extraordinary expeditionary development requiring Ultimate treatment.

events.title: A PRIVATE DISPATCH TO METELLUS CELER SETS OUT VALERIUS'S MOST SERIOUS SUSPICION
events.body: Valerius prepares a private dispatch for Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer rather than placing the full suspicion in the ordinary expedition correspondence. The dispatch reports that the road is substantially engineered, repeatedly constructed across separate inspected sections, and unexpectedly difficult to reconcile with the administrative record available to the expedition. It explicitly separates observed facts from interpretation: no deserter band, fugitive settlement, or hidden community has been identified. The private memorandum nevertheless states that, in Valerius's judgment, the most serious explanations now worth testing include the possibility of large numbers of deserters or displaced people from other communities, or a marooned and self-sustaining population that has remained outside ordinary Roman notice. The dispatch warns that either explanation would present a potentially serious problem for Roman security if evidence eventually supported it, while asking Celer to treat the suspicion as confidential until the field investigation produces firmer evidence. The sealed copy is entrusted to the established Roman correspondence channel, while the original field notes remain with the expedition.

classification_audit.reason: The confidential political dispatch is consequential and unusually candid but does not itself constitute the extraordinary discovery; it reports an unresolved hypothesis arising from the expedition's investigation.

events.title: A BLOCKED SIDE TRACK REVEALS A SECOND WAY TO LEAVE THE ENGINEERED CORRIDOR
events.body: A fresh Magnitude-11 result produces a Special event when the survey party follows one of the side approaches identified during the previous day's inspection. The track has been partly blocked by fallen material and vegetation, but beneath the obstruction the companions find a prepared turn leaving the principal engineered corridor. The feature is not sufficient to establish who used it or why it was maintained, and no hidden settlement is found beyond the inspected section. Its importance is narrower but unsettling: the engineered road was not necessarily designed as a single visible line of travel, and at least one secondary approach could allow movement away from the main corridor without immediately following the route register. The scribes record the branch separately and mark its continuation as unverified. The discovery strengthens the reason for further investigation without converting Valerius's suspicion about deserters or marooned communities into an established fact.

classification_audit.reason: The concealed side approach is significant but remains an ambiguous geographic feature without independently establishing an extraordinary hidden population, crisis, or comparable Ultimate-scale development.

events.title: THE ESTATE STEWARDS CONTINUE THE SHARED WATERING ARRANGEMENT WITHOUT ALTERING THE HOLDINGS
events.body: At the estate, the stewards continue the shared watering arrangement requested by the nearby smallholders during the previous week. The access remains within the established arrangement and produces no land transfer, payment, or change in bounded relations. Spring agricultural work continues across the existing holdings while Valerius remains away. Because agriculture is already at its recorded maximum, the continued work produces no additional agriculture point. The stewards preserve the route record so that the household's local administration remains separate from the expedition's increasingly sensitive geographic inquiry.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION HOLDS ITS POSITION WHILE THE NEW INVESTIGATION IS PREPARED FOR THE NEXT STAGE
events.body: The expedition ends the week at a temporary camp near the surveyed corridor rather than pushing farther merely to increase distance. The route sheets are divided into direct observations, traveler testimony, and unresolved hypotheses, preserving the documentary distinction already requested through the correspondence with Metellus Celer. The newly found side approach is marked for later examination, while the main engineered road remains the principal geographic thread of the expedition. The private dispatch is now on its way through the established channel, and no reply has yet arrived. The party's provisions are effectively exhausted at the present supply level, so the next movement will require deliberate logistical handling rather than another unrestricted advance. The expedition remains active, and the investigation into why such a substantial route could have escaped ordinary Roman notice is now an explicit unresolved thread.
